snippet.title: The US Sanctioned the International Criminal Court. Then Licensed Its Operations. #shorts#vantix
snippet.description:
On October 9, 2026, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control added the International Criminal Court, based in The Hague, to its sanctions list. Until then, the US had sanctioned only individual court officials. Treasury issued four general licenses at the same time: one authorizing day-to-day operations, including payments from member states and staff salaries and health insurance; one covering telecommunications and enterprise software; one covering the court’s pension plan; and one covering certain detainees. 

The State Department says the 180-day operations license is meant to give member states time to show meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions addressing US concerns about the court. That license runs to about April 7, 2027. Here’s what was designated, what was licensed, and what to watch next, with no spin.

Sources: OFAC and State Department releases, October 9, 2026. Confirm the license expiration date on OFAC’s site.

snippet.title: Trump's Treasury licensed Russian diesel imports. Four Republican senators object.
snippet.description:
Treasury's sanctions office issued General License 135 on October 9, 2026. It authorizes the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian diesel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027.

Two days later, Republican Senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis joined Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden in a joint statement. They say Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports runs directly counter to the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports, that the administration failed to consult Congress or explain its decision as required by statute, and that the United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline. They say the administration must immediately reverse course.

What this short does not claim: it does not say the license is unlawful. That is the senators' position, stated in their words and attributed to them.

Receipts:
https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20261009_33
https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/937216/download?inline
https://www.collins.senate.gov/newsroom/senator-collins-bipartisan-groups-statement-opposing-imports-of-russian-diesel

snippet.title: Inside My Legal-Limit 2 Meter Station — 1,500 Watts on VHF!
snippet.description:
Hi All!

In this video, I'm giving you a complete tour of my legal-limit 2 Meter SSB station here in western Kansas!

We'll start inside the shack with a look at the radio and amplifier, then head outside and up the tower for a closer look at the antenna system—including my 55-foot-long M2 2M8WL Yagi, mast-mounted preamp, and 7/8" Andrews HELIAX feedline. With up to 1,500 watts of transmitter power and 18.5 dBi of antenna gain, this setup can produce roughly 50,000 watts of effective radiated power (ERP) toward the horizon.

I'll also show you what this station can actually do. I routinely work a station near Wessington Springs, South Dakota—approximately 406 miles from my station in Scott City, Kansas—and I've included an actual recording of one of those remote contacts in the video.

2 Meter SSB and weak-signal VHF are quite a bit different from the FM repeater activity most people associate with the 2 Meter band. That's one of the reasons I enjoy it so much!

If you're interested in ham radio, VHF weak signal, antennas, amplifiers, station builds, and radio-related technology, consider subscribing to One Kilowatt. I'm building the channel from the ground up and have a lot more projects and station videos planned.

snippet.title: Want More Than North American POTA Contacts? Do This
snippet.description:
Want more than North American POTA contacts?

There’s a whole world waiting for you.

On this activation from the Battle of Crysler’s Farm Historic Site near Morrisburg, Ontario, the KJ6ER Challenger once again showed me just how much long-range DX is possible from a portable station when you combine the right antenna with a good understanding of propagation.
During this outing I worked three stations in Australia, including 

VK6JDW in Western Australia, along with my friend Yutaka, JH1GEX, in Japan.

Those weren’t simply lucky contacts.

Long-range portable DX becomes much more consistent when you start paying attention to which bands are opening, where propagation is favouring, what time of day you’re operating, and whether your antenna is efficiently putting your signal where you want it to go.

A lot of POTA activations understandably focus on getting the required contacts and working stations around North America. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

But if you’ve already done that and you’re wondering…

“What’s next?”

Try looking farther.

Japan. Australia. Europe. Africa. South America.

The entire world is waiting for you.

For me, that’s one of the most exciting parts of portable amateur radio. You don’t need to be sitting behind a giant home station to work serious DX. Get outside, put up an efficient antenna, understand what propagation is doing, and start listening beyond the stations you normally work.

In this video, I’m once again using the KJ6ER Challenger, a portable antenna that continues to impress me every time I take it into the field.
And this activation was also from a pretty remarkable location — the historic Battle of Crysler’s Farm, site of an important War of 1812 engagement fought on November 11, 1813.

So come along for another day of portable ham radio, history, propagation and some very satisfying long-distance contacts from Ontario, Canada.

How far have you worked from a POTA activation?

Let me know your best portable DX contact in the comments.

73,

Stuart – VE9CF

snippet.title: Why Trump Is Buying Russian Diesel From Putin (It's Not Just the Price)
snippet.description:
Why is Trump buying Russian diesel from Putin when US diesel prices just hit a record? On October 9, the president announced that Russia would ship 300,000 tons of diesel to the US, and the Treasury licensed Russian diesel imports until April 2027. Three weeks earlier, he had signed a law to punish the buyers of Russian fuel. What changed?

US diesel prices hit a record $6.53 a gallon in September. Two wars squeezed the world's diesel supply at once: the Iran war restricting the Strait of Hormuz, and Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries. Yet the United States is the world's largest diesel exporter. This documentary follows the evidence through the diesel crisis, the Russian diesel deal, Treasury General License 135, the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, the Graham sanctions law, the Miami peace talks and the energy ceasefire. Then it tests three explanations: price, politics, or Putin.

The numbers: the deal covers about 15 hours of American diesel demand, and diesel prices moved 2 cents the week after it. Here is what the evidence establishes, and what it cannot.

snippet.title: Is the 2022 Russian Oil Ban Still in Force? Congress Is Asking#shorts#vantix
snippet.description:
On October 9, 2026, the US Treasury issued a temporary general license allowing Russian diesel into the global market. On October 11, Sen. Thom Tillis told NBC’s Meet the Press there’s a legitimate case the president isn’t following the law, saying “I believe that he may be.” He pointed to a 2022 law that bans Russian oil imports unless specific conditions are met, including a full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine. Congress hasn’t changed that law. 

No court or agency has ruled on the question. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has announced a bipartisan bill to block Russian oil purchases, and Trump’s stated reason for the move is lowering diesel prices. Parts of the Russia sanctions law signed September 18 also come due October 19. Here’s what the 2022 law says, what’s been announced, and what to watch next, with no spin.

snippet.title: Why EXACTLY is India's Jamnagar being visited by America's Top Diplomat?
snippet.description:
Washington penalised India for buying Russian oil. On 9 October 2026, it licensed Russian diesel, "including importation into the United States". Days later, the State Department announced that Secretary of State Marco Rubio would travel to Samarkand, Mumbai and Jamnagar, home of Reliance's refinery complex, from 17 to 22 October.

Why EXACTLY Jamnagar? Why now? And who holds the cards as the trade deal nears the finish line and a 100% tariff law hangs in the air?

Every quote in this video is from an official source: The White House, the US State Department, India's Ministry of External Affairs, PM Narendra Modi's official channel, and Reliance Industries.

Key sources

US Treasury, OFAC General License No. 135 (9 Oct 2026): https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/937216/download
US State Department, Secretary Rubio's travel (13 Oct 2026): https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/10/secretary-rubios-travel-to-samarkand-mumbai-and-jamnagar/
International Energy Agency, Oil Market Report (14 Oct 2026): https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-october-2026
US EIA, diesel prices: https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/
PPAC, installed refining capacity: https://ppac.gov.in/infrastructure/installed-refinery-capacity
Reliance Industries, refining: https://www.ril.com/businesses/energy/refining-marketing
White House, Executive Order of 6 Feb 2026: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/02/modifying-duties-to-address-threats-to-the-united-states-by-the-government-of-the-russian-federation-04b2
MEA India, briefings and press conferences: official YouTube uploads (see the pinned comment and CREDITS)
Ship-tracking figures are from Kpler and Vortexa, as reported. "Largest and most complex single-site refinery in the world" is Reliance's own description. Figures are correct as of 16 October 2026.
